about.title: Woodlake Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Woodlake's economy runs on citrus packing, farm labor, and the small businesses that serve Tulare County's agricultural corridor. Workers here face real hazards: heavy equipment, forklifts near Valencia Boulevard loading docks, ladders in the groves, and delivery vehicles moving along Main Street. When someone is injured at work in California, workers' compensation is usually the only path against the employer, regardless of who was at fault. But that's not always the full picture. If a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver contributed to your injury, you may have a separate claim against that third party. LawProactive doesn't practice law or handle claims directly; we simply connect injured workers in Woodlake with an independent attorney who can look at the facts, explain your options honestly, and tell you whether a workers' comp claim, a third-party claim, or both may apply to your situation. There's no cost to find out.

whyChoose.title: Why Woodlake Workers Reach Out to LawProactive

items.title: Understanding Your Exclusive Remedy vs. Third-Party Rights
items.desc: California generally limits your claim against your employer to workers' compensation, but a negligent third party like a subcontractor or equipment maker may still owe you separately. An attorney can help sort out which path applies to your case.

items.title: Protecting You from Retaliation
items.desc: Reporting a workplace injury within 30 days is required, and California law prohibits employers from retaliating against you for doing so. An independent attorney can advise you if you feel you're being pushed out or punished for reporting.

items.title: Watching the Clock on Third-Party Deadlines
items.desc: If a third party contributed to your injury, that separate claim generally carries a two-year deadline in California. Missing it can close the door on compensation beyond workers' comp, so timing matters.

items.question: I was hurt working near Avenue 344 during harvest season. Can I still file a claim?
items.answer: Yes. California requires you to report a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days, so acting promptly matters. Whether it's a straightforward workers' comp claim or involves a third party like an equipment supplier, an independent attorney can review the details for free.

items.question: Does workers' compensation mean I can't sue anyone?
items.answer: Workers' comp is usually your only remedy against your employer, even if the employer was careless. However, if someone outside your employment relationship, such as a contractor or product manufacturer, contributed to your injury, you may be able to pursue a separate claim against them.

items.question: What if my employer says my injury doesn't count because I work in agriculture?
items.answer: Agricultural workers in Woodlake are generally covered by California workers' compensation just like other employees. If your employer is disputing your claim or discouraging you from reporting, an independent attorney can review your situation and explain your rights.
